sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Kettlebell RDL (Romanian Deadlift) is a hip-hinge movement that targets the hamstrings and glutes using a kettlebell held with both hands.

By hinging at the hips while maintaining a neutral spine, the movement places a deep stretch on the posterior chain and builds strength through a controlled range of motion.

This exercise is an excellent kettlebell alternative to the barbell Romanian deadlift, offering a more accessible entry point while still delivering serious hamstring and glute development.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Deep stretch and strengthening of the hamstrings and glutes
- Develops a strong hip hinge pattern essential for many lifts
- Improves posterior chain flexibility and mobility
- Lower back friendly when performed with proper form
- The kettlebell's compact shape allows a natural movement path between the legs
- Excellent for building hamstring resilience and injury prevention
- Requires minimal equipment — just one kettlebell

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Hamstrings

Secondary: Glutes, Erector Spinae, Core (Rectus Abdominis, Obliques), Forearms and Grip, Adductors

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Stand with feet hip-width apart.
2. Grip the handle of the kettlebell with both hands using an overhand grip.
3. Hold the kettlebell between your legs at around hip height.
4. Stand tall with a slight bend in your knees.
5. Pull your shoulders back and down, chest proud.
6. Your arms will remain fully extended for the duration of the movement.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Grip the handle of the kettlebell with both hands. Stand straight with the kettlebell between your legs around hip height. Your arms will remain fully extended for the duration of the movement.
2. Hinge at the hips and allow your hips to drift backward as the kettlebell goes lower to the floor. Maintain a neutral spine and pelvic position.
3. Once you reach a full stretch in your hamstrings or glutes, return back to the starting position.
4. Repeat for reps.
5. Keep the kettlebell close to your body throughout — it should travel straight down along your legs.
6. Squeeze your glutes hard at the top of each rep to fully lock out.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Rounding the lower back instead of maintaining a neutral spine
- Bending the knees too much, turning it into a squat
- Not hinging deep enough to feel the hamstring stretch
- Letting the kettlebell drift forward away from the body
- Looking up and hyperextending the neck
- Rushing through reps without controlling the eccentric (lowering) phase
- Not squeezing the glutes at the top of the movement

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Kettlebell (appropriate weight for your hip hinge strength)
- Flat, stable surface to stand on
- Optional: Exercise mat for foot traction
- Optional: Chalk for grip assistance on heavier loads
- Recommended: Start with a moderate weight to master the hinge pattern

sections.heading: Choosing Your Kettlebell Weight
sections.content:
1. Beginners: Start with 8-16 kg (men) or 4-12 kg (women).
2. Intermediate: 20-32 kg (men) or 12-20 kg (women).
3. The weight should challenge the hamstrings without compromising spinal position.
4. If your lower back rounds before you feel the hamstring stretch, reduce the weight.
5. Focus on the quality of the stretch and contraction over heavy loading.
6. Progress gradually as your hip hinge mechanics improve.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Feet: Hip-width apart, toes pointing forward or slightly out.
2. Knees: Soft bend, maintained throughout — do not increase bend during the hinge.
3. Hips: Drive backward as if closing a car door with your glutes.
4. Spine: Neutral from head to tailbone — no rounding or excessive arching.
5. Shoulders: Pulled back and down, chest open.
6. Arms: Fully extended, acting as hooks holding the kettlebell.
7. Head: Neutral, eyes looking a few feet ahead on the floor.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Barbell Romanian Deadlift: Same movement pattern with heavier loading potential
- Dumbbell RDL: Similar to kettlebell version with dumbbells at the sides
- Single Leg RDL: Unilateral version for balance and stability
- Good Morning: Barbell on back, same hip hinge pattern
- Cable Pull Through: Machine-based hip hinge with constant tension
- Stiff Leg Deadlift: Straighter legs for more hamstring isolation

sections.heading: Kettlebell RDL Variations
sections.content:
Double Hand Kettlebell RDL: Standard variation with both hands on one kettlebell
Single Arm Kettlebell RDL: One kettlebell in one hand for anti-rotation demand
Single Leg Kettlebell RDL: Unilateral version for balance and stability
Double Kettlebell RDL: One kettlebell in each hand for heavier loading
Slow Tempo Kettlebell RDL: 3-4 second eccentric for time under tension
Paused Kettlebell RDL: Pause at the bottom for stretch and strength

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Lower Back Pain: Focus on bracing the core and reduce range of motion
Hamstring Tightness: Only hinge as far as you can with a flat back, increase depth over time
Grip Fatigue: Use chalk or switch to a lighter kettlebell
Knee Issues: Maintain a consistent soft bend, avoid locking out
Balance Problems: Widen your stance slightly for more stability
Learning Stage: Practice the hip hinge with no weight first, then add the kettlebell
